Bounded Risk Point Estimation of a Normal Mean

Source: R/seq_br_norm_mean.R
seq_br_norm_mean.Rd

Given the data collected so far, checks the stopping rule of the purely sequential bounded risk point estimator of the mean of a normal population with unknown variance (Mukhopadhyay and de Silva, 2009). The aim is a sample mean whose expected loss (its risk) is no larger than a bound w chosen in advance. No fixed sample size can promise that, because the risk depends on the unknown variance, so observations are collected until the sample size reaches the size the current variance estimate calls for. The procedure is risk based, so there is no confidence level.

Usage

seq_br_norm_mean(x, A, k, w, na.rm = TRUE)

Arguments

x

Numeric vector of the observations collected so far (at least 2).

A

The loss constant: the loss from estimating the mean \(\mu\) by the sample mean is \(A\,|\bar{X}_n - \mu|^k\). A positive number; it sets the units in which the risk bound w is expressed (use A = 1 to bound the mean absolute or mean squared error itself).

k

The power in the loss: 1 for absolute error, 2 for squared error.

w

The risk bound: the largest expected loss that is acceptable. A positive number, in the units of A times the data's units to the power k.

na.rm

Logical; should NA values be removed first? Default TRUE. With FALSE, missing values are an error.

Value

An object of class c("smsd_check", "data.frame") with columns term and value and these rows:

mean

The sample mean, the point estimate.

sd

The sample standard deviation.

risk

The estimated risk at the current sample size, \(B\,(S_n^2/n)^{k/2}\).

optimal_n

The sample size the current variance estimate calls for, \(\lceil (B/w)^{2/k} S_n^2 \rceil\).

current_n

The number of observations used.

risk and optimal_n are NA when the data are constant. Attributes: is_satisfied (TRUE when current_n has reached optimal_n, which is when the estimated risk is at most w; the rounding up of optimal_n allows for rounding error of one part in \(10^{10}\), so when the estimated risk and w agree to about ten significant digits the two statements can differ, and is_satisfied is the authority), current_n, criterion_n (equal to optimal_n), method, loss_A, k, risk_bound, variance_unusable (TRUE when the data are constant, so that no variance has been estimated), and notes. conf_level and width are NULL.

Details

The function does not collect data and keeps no state. Call it after each new observation (or batch), starting once seq_br_norm_mean_pilot observations are in hand, and stop sampling the first time attr(out, "is_satisfied") is TRUE.

The loss from estimating the mean \(\mu\) by the sample mean is \(A\,|\bar{X}_n - \mu|^k\) with \(k\) equal to 1 (absolute error) or 2 (squared error). For normal data and a fixed \(n\) its expectation is $$B\,(\sigma^2/n)^{k/2}, \qquad B = A\,2^{k/2}\,\Gamma\{(k+1)/2\}/\sqrt{\pi},$$ that is, \(B = A\sqrt{2/\pi}\) for \(k = 1\) and \(B = A\) for \(k = 2\). The risk is at most w when \(n \ge n^* = (B/w)^{2/k}\sigma^2\). The sequential rule replaces \(\sigma^2\) by the sample variance \(S_n^2\): sampling stops at the first \(n\) (at or beyond the pilot size) with $$n \ge (B/w)^{2/k} S_n^2 .$$ The optimal_n row is the right hand side rounded up, and the risk row is the estimated risk at the current sample size, \(B\,(S_n^2/n)^{k/2}\); both are evaluated at the current data.

The risk bound is asymptotic. The risk of the sequential procedure approaches w as w shrinks (so that the required sample size grows), and it approaches it from above: for squared error and normal data the risk is \(A\sigma^2 E(1/N)\), where \(N\) is the final sample size, which exceeds w whenever the expected final sample size is at or below \(n^*\). With a loose bound the excess is not small. In simulation (normal data with standard deviation 3, A = 2, the pilot of seq_br_norm_mean_pilot() with its defaults, which was 10 at every bound used, 40,000 replications), the ratio of the risk to w for squared error (k = 2) was 1.11 when the bound called for 15 observations, highest, about 1.22, when it called for 25 to 30, and then 1.20, 1.05, and 1.01 when it called for 36, 100, and 400 (w of 0.5, 0.18, and 0.045). These were computed from the identity above, with a Monte Carlo standard error of at most 0.003. For absolute error (k = 1) the ratio was 1.04 at 15 observations, highest, between 1.08 and 1.09, at 25 to 30, and 1.07, 1.02, and 1.00 at 36, 100, and 400 (standard error 0.004). A larger m_0 in the pilot reduces the excess for loose bounds. ts_br_norm_mean is the two stage alternative, whose risk stays at or under the bound for normal data at the price of a larger expected sample size.

Constant data. If every observation is equal, or equal up to rounding error (a range of no more than \(10^{-10}\) times the largest absolute value, as with gain scores of 0.3 computed as posttest minus pretest), the sample variance is zero, or nothing but rounding error, and the rule as printed would be met at once. The function departs from the printed rule deliberately: no variance has been estimated, so the rule is reported as not met, risk and optimal_n are NA, attr(out, "variance_unusable") is TRUE, and a note says so (see smsd_check_methods); data whose real spread is that small beside their size should have a common value subtracted first.

Extreme units. Data that do vary, but whose spread is so large or so small that the sample variance cannot be represented in double precision (differences among the observations beyond about \(10^{154}\) or below about \(10^{-162}\)), are an error that says to change the units. That case is not reported as a rule not yet met, because collecting more data cannot help.

References

Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535

See also

seq_br_norm_mean_pilot; ts_br_norm_mean for the two stage procedure; seq_mr_norm_mean, which trades the same loss against the cost of sampling instead of bounding it.

Other seq_br_norm_mean: seq_br_norm_mean_pilot()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# Mean rating on a 7 point satisfaction scale, with a mean absolute
# error of at most 0.25 points. Ratings are simulated here as normal
# with a standard deviation of 1.2.
set.seed(113)
m <- seq_br_norm_mean_pilot(A = 1, k = 1, w = 0.25)
ratings <- rnorm(m, mean = 4.8, sd = 1.2)
out <- seq_br_norm_mean(ratings, A = 1, k = 1, w = 0.25)
out
#> Sequential check (bounded risk estimation (normal mean))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 10
#>   Criterion n     : 14
#> 
#>   mean              : 4.424481
#>   sd                : 1.145169
#>   risk              : 0.2889413
#>   optimal_n         : 14
#>   current_n         : 10
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

# Add one respondent at a time until the stopping rule is met.
while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {
  ratings <- c(ratings, rnorm(1, mean = 4.8, sd = 1.2))
  out <- seq_br_norm_mean(ratings, A = 1, k = 1, w = 0.25)
}
out
#> Sequential check (bounded risk estimation (normal mean))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 16
#>   Criterion n     : 15
#> 
#>   mean              : 4.654325
#>   sd                : 1.193281
#>   risk              : 0.2380251
#>   optimal_n         : 15
#>   current_n         : 16
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE
